What the original study did not say

The Hawthorne effect: do we improve just because we are watched?

A factory, some light bulbs and a conclusion the original data do not fully support.

Between 1924 and 1932, at Western Electric's Hawthorne Works near Chicago, researchers studied how lighting, breaks or working hours affected productivity. The popular story says output rose with any change, even when the light was dimmed, because the workers felt observed.

What the data show

When economists Steven Levitt and John List recovered the lighting data in 2011, they did not find such a clear effect: many of the rises coincided with the start of the week and other factors. Other analyses pointed out that in the relay-assembly studies less productive workers were replaced and there were financial incentives.

Still, the general idea is useful: knowing you are in a study can change behaviour. That is why trials always compare with a control group that also receives attention.

References

  1. Levitt, S. D. y List, J. A. (2011). Was there really a Hawthorne effect at the Hawthorne plant? American Economic Journal: Applied Economics, 3(1), 224–238.
  2. McCambridge, J., Witton, J. y Elbourne, D. R. (2014). Systematic review of the Hawthorne effect. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 67(3), 267–277.
